name: The Amalekite who claimed to kill Saul
charge: Claiming to have slain the Lord's anointed
summary: A young Amalekite came to David at Ziklag with Saul's crown and bracelet and said he had killed the wounded king at his own request. The earlier chapter says Saul fell on his own sword. Either way, his mouth condemned him.
offense: The messenger arrived with torn clothes and earth upon his head, bringing news that Saul and Jonathan were dead. David required him to explain how he knew. He said he had found Saul in anguish upon Gilboa, had killed him at his request, and had taken the crown and bracelet to bring to David (2 Samuel 1:1-10). The ornaments were presented as the tokens of a deed from which he expected advantage. David did not receive the report as the happy removal of a rival. He and his men mourned, wept, and fasted for Saul, Jonathan, and the fallen of Israel (2 Samuel 1:11-12). The throne's opening did not make the nation's loss a cause for celebration. The man who had refused to kill Saul in the cave and camp was not about to reward another for claiming the act (1 Samuel 24:6; 26:9-11). David asked why the messenger had not feared to stretch forth his hand against the Lord's anointed (2 Samuel 1:13-14). The man's appeal to Saul's request and approaching death did not persuade him that killing the king was a service. He had offered his own account as evidence, and the judgment was returned upon that testimony.
judgment: David ordered one of his young men to fall upon him. The sentence expressly rested on what he had said: his mouth had testified that he slew the Lord's anointed (2 Samuel 1:15-16). He brought Saul's crown expecting the new king's favour and instead received judgment for the act he claimed.

The ornaments were presented as the tokens of a deed from which he expected advantage.

David did not receive the report as the happy removal of a rival. He and his men mourned, wept, and fasted for Saul, Jonathan, and the fallen of Israel (2 Samuel 1:11-12). The throne's opening did not make the nation's loss a cause for celebration. David asked why the messenger had not feared to stretch forth his hand against the Lord's anointed (2 Samuel 1:13-14). entries.commentary: After the death of Saul, when David had returned from the slaughter of the Amalekites and abode two days in Ziklag, a man came out of the camp of Israel with his clothes rent and earth upon his head, and fell to the earth before David to do him honor. David asked him how the matter went, and he answered that the people were fled from the battle, many had fallen and were dead, and Saul and Jonathan his son were dead also.

The young man told David that he had come by chance upon mount Gilboa, and found Saul leaning upon his spear with the chariots and horsemen pressing hard after him. In the earlier account Saul fell upon his sword but did not die at that moment. The man said he was an Amalekite, and that Saul asked him to stand upon him and slay him because anguish was come upon him; so he slew him, being sure he could not live, and took the crown from his head and the bracelet from his arm and brought them to David. The Amalekites are the seed of Esau, of Eliphaz his son. Their lineage is written in Genesis, and it is a thing to know when reading of Israel's enemies.

David took hold on his clothes and rent them, and all the men with him did likewise, and they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul, for Jonathan, and for the house of Israel that were fallen by the sword. The renting of garments was the sign of mourning, but the Most High looks for a rent heart and not rent garments only; true repentance is inward, not just an outward show. David asked the man how he was not afraid to stretch forth his hand to destroy the Lord's anointed. Even a man about to die was not to be touched; the judgment of the Lord was to be let play out. David then commanded one of his young men to fall upon the Amalekite, and he died, for his own mouth had testified against him.

David lamented over Saul and over Jonathan, and bade them teach the children of Judah the use of the bow, which is written in the book of Jasher. The book of Jasher is not in the canon because the Most High did not will us to have it; He put in the book exactly what He wanted His people to read in the last days. This walk in the last days is not by might nor by power but by the Spirit of the Lord. The captivity is not overthrown by rising up with the bow or the gun; this is spiritual war and not physical. There is nothing wrong with knowing how to defend yourself, but the redemption of Israel does not come by force of arms. David's lament is a prophecy given in the spirit, almost a eulogy: Saul and Jonathan were lovely and pleasant in their lives, and in their death they were not divided; they were swifter than eagles and stronger than lions. Before the devil jumped on Saul he was good, and the two of them were good together. Israel's forefathers died only when the Most High said it was time; that is the only way any of them died. David mourned Jonathan, saying his love to him was wonderful, passing the love of women.

Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled from before the Philistines and fell down slain in mount Gilboa. The Philistines followed hard upon Saul and upon his sons, and slew Jonathan, and Abinadab, and Malchishua, Saul's sons. The battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him, and he was sore wounded of the archers.

Saul said unto his armourbearer, Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me. What Saul was fearful of is what you see in war, how men will abuse their captives, killing them and abusing their bodies. He was already wounded and could not get away, so instead of being taken captive he told his armourbearer to kill him. His armourbearer would not, for he was sore afraid; therefore Saul took a sword and fell upon it, and when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise upon his sword and died with him. So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armourbearer, and all his men, that same day together. Remember what we read in chapter 28: when Saul went and conjured up the spirit of Samuel, Samuel said to him, To morrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me. He prophesied unto Saul what was going to happen, and now we read the fulfillment of that prophecy.

When the men of Israel that were on the other side of the valley, and they that were on the other side of Jordan, saw that the men of Israel fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they forsook the cities and fled, and the Philistines came and dwelt in them.

On the morrow, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen in mount Gilboa. They cut off his head and stripped off his armour, and sent into the land of the Philistines round about, to publish it in the house of their idols and among the people. They put his armour in the house of Ashtaroth, and they fastened his body to the wall of Bethshan.

When the inhabitants of Jabeshgilead heard of that which the Philistines had done to Saul, all the valiant men arose and went all night, and took the body of Saul and the bodies of his sons from the wall of Bethshan, and came to Jabesh and burnt them there. They took their bones and buried them under a tree at Jabesh, and fasted seven days. So in chapter 31 we read of Saul and his sons and his armourbearer dying at the hands of the Philistines. This concludes the history of Saul coming to an end; the second book of Samuel takes up the rise and much of the history concerning King David. --- Topics: [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

Coming out of the prior chapters, Saul was hunting after David to kill him. When Saul returned from following the Philistines and was told David was in the wilderness of Engedi, he took three thousand chosen men out of all Israel to seek David and his men upon the rocks of the wild goats. Saul went into the cave to cover his feet: that means he was in there relieving himself. See the vulnerable position Saul was in, and yet David spared his life; that is why David could say, thou wast delivered into my hand, but I did not take thy life.

Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand: who is being referred to as the enemy? His own people; Saul was of the tribe of Benjamin, and David was of the tribe of Judah. On the skirt: the Zondervan Compact Bible Dictionary (page 136) shows the basic garments in general use among men of biblical times were the inner tunic, the tunic coat, the girdle, and the cloak, with the headdress and sandals. The word skirt in the KJV usually refers to an article of male, not female, clothing, with meanings of extremity and corner. Where we have our fringes attached to the borders of our garments, that is the bottom part of Saul's robe that David cut off privily.

When Saul rose out of the cave, David went out after him, cried, My lord the king, and stooped with his face to the earth and bowed himself. He reverenced Saul even though Saul was trying to kill him; that is why the Most High said David is a man after mine own heart. David maintained his integrity. David laid the proof before Saul: this day thine eyes have seen how the Lord delivered thee into mine hand in the cave, and some bade me kill thee, but mine eye spared thee, for he is the Lord's anointed. See the skirt of thy robe in my hand: I cut off the skirt and killed thee not; there is neither evil nor transgression in mine hand, yet thou huntest my soul to take it. David left the judgment with the Most High: the Lord judge between me and thee, and the Lord avenge me of thee, but mine hand shall not be upon thee; as saith the proverb of the ancients, Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked. After whom is the king of Israel come out? after a dead dog, after a flea.

Saul lifted up his voice and wept, and said to David, Thou art more righteous than I, for thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil; if a man find his enemy, will he let him go well away? Saul made an acknowledgement there because he saw the righteousness of David: I know well that thou shalt surely be king, and that the kingdom of Israel shall be established in thine hand.

Saul asked David to swear that he would not cut off his seed after him nor destroy his name out of his father's house, and David sware unto Saul; Saul went home, and David and his men gat them up unto the hold. David showed so much restraint and respect unto his elder; that is something some of us struggle with today, and we need to use this as an example. The Most High was dealing with David: even though he saw Saul acting wickedly and strangely with him, when he had the opportunity to kill Saul he would not do it.

The Ziphites came unto Saul to Gibeah, saying, Doth not David hide himself in the hill of Hachilah, which is before Jeshimon? Right here we are going back: chapter 26 is picking up on what we read in chapter 23, when the Ziphites first went up to Saul to deliver David into the king's hand.

David beheld the place where Saul lay, with Abner the son of Ner, the captain of his host; Saul lay in the trench with his spear stuck in the ground at his bolster, and the people pitched round about him as protection to the king. David asked Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai the son of Zeruiah, the brother of Joab, Who will go down with me to Saul to the camp? and Abishai said, I will go down with thee; and they came to the people by night, and all lay sleeping.

Abishai said, God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand this day; let me smite him, I pray thee, with the spear even to the earth at once, and I will not smite him the second time. But David said, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the Lord's anointed, and be guiltless? David left Saul's end with the Most High: as the Lord liveth, the Lord shall smite him, or his day shall come to die, or he shall descend into battle and perish; the Lord forbid that I should stretch forth mine hand against the Lord's anointed. They took the spear and the cruse of water from Saul's bolster and got them away, and no man saw it, nor knew it, neither awaked, for they were all asleep, because a deep sleep from the Lord was fallen upon them.

David went over to the other side, stood on the top of an hill afar off, and cried to Abner: Art not thou a valiant man? and who is like to thee in Israel? wherefore then hast thou not kept thy lord the king? for there came one of the people in to destroy the king thy lord. As the Lord liveth, ye are worthy to die, because ye have not kept your master, the Lord's anointed; and now see where the king's spear is, and the cruse of water that was at his bolster.

Saul knew David's voice and said, Is this thy voice, my son David? And David said, Wherefore doth my lord thus pursue after his servant? for what have I done? or what evil is in mine hand? Let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the Lord: for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains.

Saul said, I have sinned: return, my son David, for I will no more do thee harm, because my soul was precious in thine eyes this day: behold, I have played the fool, and have erred exceedingly. Saul was acknowledging once more David's righteousness, because again David had an opportunity to kill Saul and did not put forth his hand. David answered, The Lord render to every man his righteousness and his faithfulness: for the Lord delivered thee into my hand to day, but I would not stretch forth mine hand against the Lord's anointed. Again he showed compassion, restraint, and the fear of the Most High. That is what we have to get to as far as brotherly love: when we see each other, we see Christ in each other. That is what our nation is lacking, and that is why we have to be that example, as David was in sparing Saul's life.

verses.text: It came even to pass on the third day, that, behold, a man came out of the camp from Saul with his clothes rent, and earth upon his head: and so it was, when he came to David, that he fell to the earth, and did obeisance.
And David said unto him, From whence comest thou? And he said unto him, Out of the camp of Israel am I escaped.

And David said unto him, How went the matter? I pray thee, tell me. And he answered, That the people are fled from the battle, and many of the people also are fallen and dead; and Saul and Jonathan his son are dead also.
And David said unto the young man that told him, How knowest thou that Saul and Jonathan his son be dead?
And the young man that told him said, As I happened by chance upon mount Gilboa, behold, Saul leaned upon his spear; and, lo, the chariots and horsemen followed hard after him.
And when he looked behind him, he saw me, and called unto me. And I answered, Here am I.
And he said unto me, Who art thou? And I answered him, I am an Amalekite.
He said unto me again, Stand, I pray thee, upon me, and slay me: for anguish is come upon me, because my life is yet whole in me.

So I stood upon him, and slew him, because I was sure that he could not live after that he was fallen: and I took the crown that was upon his head, and the bracelet that was on his arm, and have brought them hither unto my lord.
And David said unto the young man that told him, Whence art thou? And he answered, I am the son of a stranger, an Amalekite.
And David said unto him, How wast thou not afraid to stretch forth thine hand to destroy the Lord’s anointed?
And David called one of the young men, and said, Go near, and fall upon him. And he smote him that he died.
And David said unto him, Thy blood be upon thy head; for thy mouth hath testified against thee, saying, I have slain the Lord’s anointed.
And the battle went sore against Saul, and the archers hit him; and he was sore wounded of the archers.

Then said Saul unto his armourbearer, Draw thy sword, and thrust me through therewith; lest these uncircumcised come and thrust me through, and abuse me. But his armourbearer would not; for he was sore afraid. Therefore Saul took a sword, and fell upon it.
And when his armourbearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell likewise upon his sword, and died with him.
And he said unto his men, The Lord forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, the Lord’s anointed, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the anointed of the Lord.
And David said to Abishai, Destroy him not: for who can stretch forth his hand against the Lord’s anointed, and be guiltless?
David said furthermore, As the Lord liveth, the Lord shall smite him; or his day shall come to die; or he shall descend into battle, and perish.
The Lord forbid that I should stretch forth mine hand against the Lord’s anointed: but, I pray thee, take thou now the spear that is at his bolster, and the cruse of water, and let us go.
